summary: This experimental document proposes raising TCP's permitted initial window from between 2 and 4 segments to 10 segments, falling back to the older recommendation if problems appear. It explains the motivation, weighs the pros and cons, and reports large-scale experiments in which the larger window improved performance for many web services.

plainLanguage.summary: When two computers open a connection, the first one starts by sending a small amount and waits for a reply before sending more. RFC 6928 allows that first amount to be larger, up to ten packets instead of between two and four. The document reports large-scale tests showing that pages and searches load faster, at the cost of a slightly higher rate of retransmissions, and asks operators to measure before and after turning it on.

subtitle: Why TCP's first burst of data was allowed to grow from 2 to 4 segments up to 10, and what to watch for when doing it.

tldr.problem: A new TCP connection may send only 2 to 4 segments before hearing back, which wastes round trips on the short transfers that dominate web traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC raises the upper bound on the initial window to 10 segments, with a cap of 14600 bytes, and asks anyone enabling it to monitor results and fall back to the RFC 3390 value if problems appear.
tldr.outcome: This is an Experimental RFC. Google's large-scale tests showed lower latency with a small rise in retransmissions, but it asks for more experiments before the change becomes the default.

today: RFC 6928 is an Experimental document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It asks for further experiments before a larger initial window is enabled by default, and says that a follow-up document may revisit the question if no significant harm is reported. The measurements it reports came from Google's own front-end infrastructure, described in the companion papers it cites, and it closes by reporting the consensus of the TCP Maintenance and Minor Extensions working group on near-term use of the larger window.

sections.title: The Proposal in Brief
sections.content:
The document proposes to raise the upper bound on TCP's initial window to 10 segments, with a maximum of 14600 bytes. It is patterned after and borrows heavily from RFC 3390 and earlier work in the area. Because of lingering concerns about possible side effects on other flows that share the same network bottleneck, some of the recommendations are conditional on additional monitoring and evaluation.

The primary argument in favour of raising the initial window follows from the growing scale of the Internet. Ten segments are likely to fit into the queue space available at any broadband access link, even when there are a reasonable number of concurrent connections. Lower speed links can be treated with environment-specific configurations, so that they are protected from being overwhelmed by large initial window bursts without imposing a suboptimal initial window on the rest of the Internet.

The authors recommend that all TCP implementations have a settable initial window parameter, as long as there is a reasonable effort to monitor for possible interactions with other Internet applications and services. The document explains why 10 segments may be an appropriate value and notes that while that value may continue to rise in the future, it includes no supporting evidence for values larger than 10. It also introduces a minor revision to RFC 3390 and RFC 5681 to eliminate resetting the initial window when the SYN or SYN/ACK is lost.
sections.plainLanguage: The change is small and easy to undo: one number that says how much a new connection may send before it waits for a reply. The authors want it to be configurable and want anyone who changes it to keep watching the effect.

sections.title: The Modified Initial Window Rule
sections.content:
The upper bound for the initial window becomes min (10*MSS, max (2*MSS, 14600)), where MSS is the maximum segment size. This is a change from RFC 3390, which specified that the congestion window be initialized between 2 and 4 segments depending on the MSS. The increase is optional: a TCP may start with a smaller window. The change applies to the initial window of the connection in the first round trip time of data transmission during or following the three-way handshake, and neither the SYN/ACK nor its ACK should increase the initial window size.

The memo notes that all its test results were based on the regular Ethernet MTU of 1500 bytes, and that further study of a different MTU may be needed. It also changes one related rule. RFC 3390 said that if the SYN or SYN/ACK is lost, the initial window used by a sender after a correctly transmitted SYN must be one segment of MSS bytes. Because the default retransmission timeout was reduced to 1 second, the chance of a spurious SYN or SYN/ACK retransmission grew, which would unnecessarily penalise connections with a round trip time over 1 second. The recommendation is therefore to refrain from resetting the initial window to 1 segment unless there have been more than one SYN or SYN/ACK retransmission or true loss has been detected.

TCP implementations use slow start in up to three ways: to start a new connection, which is the initial window; to restart transmission after a long idle period, which is the restart window; and to restart transmission after a retransmission timeout, which is the loss window. This document changes only the initial window. Optionally, a TCP may set the restart window to the smaller of the initial window value and the current value of the congestion window, so that a larger restart window never increases the congestion window. The loss window is unchanged and must remain one segment of MSS bytes. To limit the negative effect on links with little bandwidth or buffer space, implementations should fall back to the RFC 3390 value for the restart window if any packet loss is detected during either the initial window or a restart window and more than 4 KB of data is sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the very first burst changes. The window used after a long pause and the window used after a timeout are separate settings, and the one used after a timeout stays at a single segment so that a congested link can still back off hard.

sections.title: Why a Bigger Window Helps
sections.content:
An increase of the initial window from 3 segments to 10 segments reduces the total transfer time for data sets greater than 4 KB by up to 4 round trips. The memo tabulates the round trips needed for each transfer size, assuming infinite bandwidth, no packet loss and standard delayed acknowledgements. With the larger initial window, a transfer of 32 segments of data needs 2 round trips rather than 5.

The second reason is that web objects have grown. RFC 3390's main motivation for raising the initial window to 4 KB was to speed up connections that only transmit a small amount of data, and back then most transfers were under 4 KB and could be completed in a single round trip. Today only a small percentage of web objects can fit in the 4 KB initial window: the memo gives the example that 10% of Google's search responses fit, and that the average HTTP response size of gmail.com is 8 KB.

The third reason is faster recovery from loss on under-used or wireless links. An initial window larger than 3 segments increases the chance that a lost packet is recovered through fast retransmit rather than the lengthy initial retransmission timeout, because fast retransmit needs three duplicate acknowledgements to decide that a segment was lost rather than reordered.
sections.plainLanguage: A bigger first burst means the data arrives in fewer round trips. That matters most for the short exchanges the web is made of, and it also means a lost packet is more likely to be spotted quickly than waiting for a timeout.

sections.title: Risks and Mitigations
sections.content:
The larger bursts may cause buffer overrun and packet drop in routers with small buffers or routers experiencing congestion, which could result in unnecessary retransmission timeouts and an unnecessarily early transition from the slow start to the congestion avoidance phase. Premature drops are unlikely in uncongested networks with sufficient buffering, or in moderately congested networks where the congested router uses active queue management such as Random Early Detection. Insufficient buffering is more likely at the access routers connecting slower links: a study of access router buffer sizes found that the majority provision enough buffer for 130 ms or longer, which is sufficient to cover a burst of more than 10 packets at 1 Mbps, but possibly not sufficient for browsers opening simultaneous connections. A testbed study with five simultaneously opened connections found that even with limited buffer size on slow links, the larger window still reduced the total latency of web transactions, at the cost of higher packet drop rates.

For the network as a whole, the increase happens once, at the start of a connection, and the rest of TCP's backoff machinery stays in place, so the memo argues it is unlikely to leave a network in a persistent state of congestion or cause a collapse. That may not hold if applications open a large number of simultaneous connections, and until the change is widely deployed there may be a fairness issue between flows that use the larger window and flows that still follow RFC 3390.

Recent measurements also report extremely large queues, of the order of a second or more, at access networks, and queuing delay is generally considered harmful for latency-sensitive traffic such as DNS queries, ARP, DHCP, Voice over IP and gaming. The larger window can make that worse during short downloads. The memo's mitigation is for hosts directly connected to a low-speed link to advertise an initial receive window smaller than 10 segments, either by manual configuration or by detecting the low-bandwidth link.
sections.plainLanguage: The risk is that a burst of ten packets overruns a small buffer somewhere and gets dropped, which slows things down rather than speeding them up. The main cases where that bites are slow links and hosts running many connections at once.

sections.title: Large-Scale Test Results
sections.content:
The memo reports experiments run through Google's front-end infrastructure serving a diverse set of applications, in two data centres. AvgDC has connection bandwidths closer to the worldwide average, with a median connection speed of about 1.7 Mbps. SlowDC has a larger proportion of traffic from slow-bandwidth subnets, with nearly 20% of traffic from connections below 100 Kbps.

The average web search latency improvement over all responses is 11.7% in AvgDC and 8.7% in SlowDC. The improvement held across a variety of subnets, with the largest benefits of over 20% on high round trip time and high bandwidth-delay product networks where most responses fit within the pipe, and the smallest, about 5%, on low round trip time paths. Contrary to what the authors expected, responses from low-bandwidth subnets saw the best improvements, between 10% and 20% in the 0-56 Kbps and 56-256 Kbps buckets. At the granularity of a single /24 subnet, latency improved at all quantiles, ranging from 5% to 11%.

The cost is a modest rise in retransmissions. The overall increase is 0.3% in AvgDC, from 1.98% to 2.29%, and 0.7% in SlowDC, from 3.54% to 4.21%. With one exception, the larger window raised the retransmission rate of services in AvgDC by less than 0.5%. The exception was the Maps application, which runs many concurrent TCP connections and rose by 0.9% in AvgDC and 1.85% in SlowDC, from 3.94% to 5.79%. In the worst case examined, the 99th percentile latency for Maps in SlowDC rose by 2.3%, which is 80 ms.
sections.plainLanguage: On the authors' own network the change made searches about 9% to 12% faster, and the retransmission rate rose by less than one percentage point. The exception was a map application running many connections at once, which paid a bit more.

sections.title: Deployment Guidance
sections.content:
Further experiments are required before a larger initial window is enabled by default on the Internet. The existing measurement results indicate that this does not cause significant harm to other traffic, but widespread use could reveal issues not yet known, such as fairness or an impact on latency-sensitive traffic such as VoIP. Special care is therefore needed, particularly on large-scale systems originating a significant amount of Internet traffic and on large numbers of individual systems with a similar aggregate impact.

Anyone turning on a larger initial window should ensure that performance is monitored before and after the change. The key metrics are the rate of packet losses, ECN marking and segment retransmissions during the initial burst. The sender should cache information about connection setups that used a window larger than RFC 3390 allows, and new connections should fall back to the RFC 3390 window if there is evidence of performance problems. An increased initial window must not be turned on by default on systems without such monitoring capabilities. If users observe significant deterioration, they should fall back to the RFC 3390 window for safety reasons.

The memo closes by saying that if no significant harm is reported, a follow-up document may revisit whether a larger initial window can safely be used by default in all Internet hosts, and that resolving the experiments and tightening the suggestions here might be grounds for a future Standards Track document.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not switch this on by default. Measure the loss rate and the retransmission rate before and after, keep a note of connections that used the bigger window, and be ready to drop back to the old value.

items.title: Initial window
items.text: Changed by this document: the upper bound rises to 10 segments.

items.title: Restart window
items.text: Optional: may be set to the smaller of the initial window and the current congestion window.

items.title: Loss window
items.text: Unchanged: it stays at one segment of MSS bytes, so a congested link can still back off hard.
